title: The Effect of Gut-Training and Feeding-Challenge on Markers of Gastrointestinal Status in Response to Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Literature Review
authors: Martinez IG, Mika AS, Biesiekierski JR, Costa RJS
population: Eight studies of gut-training or feeding-challenge (7 carbohydrate only, 1 carbohydrate plus protein), 4-28 day interventions, cycling or running
findings: 304 studies identified, 8 included; quality assessed with RoB 2.
Gut discomfort decreased by an average of 47% after 2-week repetitive carbohydrate feeding (n = 2) and 26% with repeated fluid ingestion over five trials (n = 1).
Carbohydrate malabsorption fell 45-54% in two studies of 2-week carbohydrate feeding but did not change significantly in one.

Significant improvements in GI symptoms in 2 studies, unclear in 4; no significant change in gastric emptying (n = 2) or intestinal injury/permeability markers (n = 3); cytokine results inconclusive (n = 2).
Conclusion: gut-training may reduce gut discomfort and potentially improve carbohydrate malabsorption and Ex-GIS, with possible performance implications.
limitations: Eight small heterogeneous studies, mostly CHO-only and short; no ultra-distance trials; mixed symptom tools.
implications: Gut-training is plausible but low-certainty: offer as an optional 2-4 week progression, not a mandatory block.
Raise CHO progressively during long runs and stop progression when GI symptoms worsen (step size is an engine default, not from the evidence).
Intestinal injury markers did not change: do not claim gut-training protects the gut barrier.

verification.notes: Crossref match; all numbers confirmed in the Europe PMC abstract. The '~10 g/h steps' in the researcher's implication is not from the paper and was removed from the evidence claims.
